Municipal wastewater (sewage) treatment occurs in two major stages: primary (physical) treatment and secondary (biological) treatment, followed by anaerobic digestion of activated sludge.

Step 2: Evaluation
Primary treatment physically removes floating debris by sequential filtration and removes grit (soil and small pebbles) by sedimentation, making the description of primary treatment correct. During secondary treatment, the primary effluent is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped into it, allowing vigorous growth of useful aerobic microbes into flocs (masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments). These microbes consume the major part of the organic matter in the effluent, which significantly reduces—rather than increases—the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) of the effluent; thus, the claim that BOD increases is incorrect. Finally, when activated sludge is pumped into anaerobic sludge digesters, anaerobic bacteria digest the microbes in the sludge and produce biogas containing methane, hydrogen sulphide, and carbon dioxide, making this description correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the descriptions of primary physical treatment and anaerobic sludge digestion are correct, while the claim regarding an increase in BOD during secondary aerobic treatment is incorrect.

name.text: [ch008-unit-8-biology-and-human-welfare] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_AR_Q05 - Contact inhibition and metastasis in cancer

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Cancerous cells lose the property of contact inhibition and continue to divide, giving rise to masses of cells called tumours.

Reason (R): Metastasis is the most feared property of benign tumours, in which cells slough off from the tumour and reach distant sites through blood to start new tumours.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal cells exhibit a regulatory property called contact inhibition, whereby contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancerous transformation disrupts this regulation.

Step 2: Evaluation
In normal tissues, cell division is tightly controlled, whereas cancer cells lose contact inhibition and divide uncontrollably to form neoplastic masses called tumours. Therefore, the assertion regarding loss of contact inhibition and tumour formation is correct. Tumours are of two types: benign and malignant. Benign tumours normally remain confined to their original location, do not spread to other parts of the body, and cause little damage. In contrast, malignant tumours consist of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow rapidly, invade surrounding normal tissues, and slough off to reach distant sites via blood—a property called metastasis. Attributing metastasis to benign tumours is therefore incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, whereas the reason is incorrect because metastasis is a characteristic property of malignant tumours rather than benign tumours.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: [ch008-unit-8-biology-and-human-welfare] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SBM_Q06 - Pathogens, drugs, and microbial biocontrol agents

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements carefully:

  • Typhoid fever, caused by the pathogenic bacterium Salmonella typhi, can be confirmed by the Widal test.
  • Wuchereria bancrofti causes slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs in which it lives for many years, usually the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs.
  • Morphine is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum and is a very effective sedative and painkiller.
  • Baculoviruses used as biological control agents belong to the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus and are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticidal applications.
  • Rhizobium is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium commonly used as a biofertilizer in flooded paddy fields.

How many of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human diseases, pharmacological agents, biocontrol organisms, and biofertilizers each have specific causative microbes, plant sources, or ecological relationships.

Step 2: Evaluation
First, Salmonella typhi is indeed the bacterium responsible for typhoid fever, and its infection is clinically confirmed using the Widal test; this is correct. Second, the filarial worm Wuchereria bancrofti causes elephantiasis (filariasis), characterized by chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs; this is correct. Third, morphine is an opioid extracted from the latex of Papaver somniferum and serves as an effective clinical sedative and analgesic; this is correct. Fourth, baculoviruses in the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods and are ideal for integrated pest management due to their species-specific, narrow-spectrum action with no negative impacts on non-target organisms; this is correct. Fifth, Rhizobium forms symbiotic associations within the root nodules of leguminous plants rather than acting as a free-living nitrogen fixer in paddy fields (where cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc, and Oscillatoria serve as important biofertilizers); hence, this last claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Out of the five statements, four statements are biologically accurate and one is incorrect.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Activation of Bt toxin in insect gut

questiontext.text: Why does the Bt toxin protein produced by Bacillus thuringiensis not kill the bacterium itself, but kills the target insect upon ingestion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce insecticidal protein crystals during a particular phase of their growth. These proteins exist as inactive protoxins inside the bacterium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Once an insect ingests the inactive protoxin, it is converted into an active form of toxin due to the alkaline pH of the insect midgut, which solubilizes the crystals. The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis, eventually leading to the death of the insect. Because the bacterial cytoplasm does not provide the alkaline conditions required for solubilization and activation, the bacterium remains unharmed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin in the bacterium and becomes activated only in the alkaline pH of the insect gut.

answer.text: The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin in the bacterium and is activated by the alkaline pH of the insect gut.
The bacterial cell wall is impermeable to the active toxin, whereas the acidic insect gut degrades the insect cuticle.
The bacterium synthesizes an antitoxin that neutralizes the active toxin inside its own cytoplasm.
The protoxin requires host insect DNA polymerase to be transcribed into an active toxin inside the midgut.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Gene therapy for ADA deficiency

questiontext.text: In the first clinical gene therapy given to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, why did the patient require periodic infusions of genetically engineered lymphocytes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gene therapy attempts to correct a hereditary disease by delivering a normal functional gene into the individual's cells or tissues. ADA deficiency is caused by the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase, an enzyme crucial for the immune system to function.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the 1990 clinical gene therapy trial, lymphocytes from the patient's blood were grown in culture outside the body, a functional ADA cDNA was introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, and the cells were subsequently returned to the patient. However, mature lymphocytes are not immortal and have a finite lifespan. Consequently, the patient required periodic infusions of such genetically engineered lymphocytes. A permanent cure could only be achieved if the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Periodic infusions were required because the genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal and have a limited lifespan.

answer.text: The retroviral vector is degraded by restriction enzymes inside the patient's bone marrow within a few days.
Adenosine deaminase enzyme permanently inhibits the replication of genetically modified T-cells.
The genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal and have a finite lifespan in the body.
The functional ADA cDNA cannot be transcribed in human cells without continuous antibiotic selection.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SB2_Q09 - Recombinant human insulin synthesis by Eli Lilly

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements regarding recombinant human insulin:

Statement I: In mammals, insulin is synthesized as a pro-hormone containing an extra stretch called the C-peptide, which is removed during maturation into functional insulin consisting of A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges.

Statement II: In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared three DNA sequences corresponding to A, B, and C chains of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of Escherichia coli to produce all three chains separately before joining them.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains—chain A and chain B—linked together by disulphide bridges. In mammals, it is initially synthesized as a pro-hormone containing an additional C-peptide that is absent in mature insulin.

Step 2: Evaluation
The description of mammalian pro-insulin maturation—where the C-peptide is cleaved off leaving the A and B chains joined by disulphide bonds—is accurate. However, the main challenge in producing insulin using recombinant DNA technology was assembling insulin into its mature form without the C-peptide. In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared only two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin (not the C chain) and introduced them into plasmids of Escherichia coli to produce the A and B chains separately, which were then extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin. Therefore, the claim that Eli Lilly synthesized and joined the C chain is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement describing pro-insulin maturation is correct, whereas the statement claiming that Eli Lilly prepared DNA sequences for all three chains including the C chain is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SB3_Q10 - Restriction enzymes, electrophoresis, and insertional inactivation

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding tools of recombinant DNA technology:

  1. The restriction endonuclease EcoRI recognizes the palindromic sequence \(5'\text{-GAATTC-}3'\) and cuts each of the two strands of the DNA double helix between G and A bases, producing sticky ends.
  2. During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments being positively charged move towards the cathode under an electric field, with larger fragments moving farther than smaller ones.
  3. Insertional inactivation of the \(\beta\)-galactosidase coding sequence in a recombinant plasmid results in colonies that do not produce any blue colour in the presence of a chromogenic substrate.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Recombinant DNA technology relies on restriction endonucleases for specific DNA cleavage, agarose gel electrophoresis for size-based separation of DNA fragments, and selectable markers (such as chromogenic enzyme genes) for identifying recombinants.

Step 2: Evaluation
First, EcoRI recognizes the palindromic sequence \(5'\text{-GAATTC-}3'\) and cleaves the sugar-phosphate backbone between the G and A residues on both strands, leaving overhanging single-stranded stretches called sticky ends; this is correct. Second, DNA molecules are negatively charged due to their phosphate backbone, so during gel electrophoresis they migrate towards the positive electrode (anode), and the sieving effect of the agarose gel causes smaller fragments to move farther than larger ones; therefore, claiming that DNA is positively charged and moves towards the cathode with larger fragments moving farther is incorrect. Third, when a recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme \(\beta\)-galactosidase, the gene is inactivated (insertional inactivation), so the bacterial colonies fail to produce the enzyme and remain colourless rather than turning blue in the presence of a chromogenic substrate; this is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The descriptions of EcoRI cleavage and insertional inactivation of \(\beta\)-galactosidase are correct, while the description of DNA migration in agarose gel electrophoresis is incorrect.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_DIAG_Q11 - Selection of recombinants in pBR322 cloning vector

questiontext.text: Observe the schematic diagram of the cloning vector pBR322 shown below. If a foreign DNA fragment is ligated at the BamHI restriction site, what will be the growth phenotype of the host E. coli cells carrying this recombinant plasmid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic depicts the plasmid cloning vector pBR322 containing the origin of replication (ori), the ampicillin resistance gene (ampR) with PstI and PvuI sites, and the tetracycline resistance gene (tetR) with BamHI and SalI sites. A foreign DNA fragment is ligated into the BamHI site.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In plasmid selection, an intact antibiotic resistance gene confers survival on medium containing that specific antibiotic, whereas insertion of foreign DNA within the coding region of an antibiotic resistance gene disrupts its function through insertional inactivation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By the principle of insertional inactivation of selectable markers, inserting foreign DNA at a restriction site located inside a resistance gene renders the host cell sensitive to that antibiotic while preserving resistance conferred by any other intact marker gene on the vector.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because the BamHI restriction site lies within the tetracycline resistance gene (tetR), ligating foreign DNA at this site disrupts the tetR gene, causing the recombinant plasmid to lose tetracycline resistance. Meanwhile, the ampicillin resistance gene (ampR) remains intact and functional. Consequently, transformed E. coli cells carrying this recombinant plasmid will survive and grow on ampicillin-containing medium, but will fail to grow when transferred to tetracycline-containing medium.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Non-recombinant transformants remain resistant to both ampicillin and tetracycline, whereas recombinants with insertion at BamHI are resistant only to ampicillin and sensitive to tetracycline. Therefore, the host cells will grow on ampicillin-containing medium but not on tetracycline-containing medium.

answer.text: They will grow on both ampicillin-containing and tetracycline-containing media.
They will fail to grow on both ampicillin-containing and tetracycline-containing media.
They will grow on tetracycline-containing medium, but not on ampicillin-containing medium.
They will grow on ampicillin-containing medium, but not on tetracycline-containing medium.

name.text: [ch009-unit-9-biotechnology-and-its-applications] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQ_Q12 - Chronological steps of recombinant DNA technology

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps of recombinant DNA technology in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Ligation of the desired DNA fragment into a cloning vector
  2. Fragmentation of isolated DNA by restriction endonucleases
  3. Isolation of pure genetic material (DNA) from the source cell
  4. Transferring the recombinant DNA into a suitable host organism
  5. Isolation of the desired DNA fragment using agarose gel electrophoresis

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The construction and expression of a recombinant DNA molecule follows a defined laboratory workflow from nucleic acid extraction to host transformation.

Step 2: Evaluation
First, pure DNA must be isolated from the source organism by lysing cells and removing macromolecules such as RNA, proteins, and polysaccharides. Second, the purified DNA is cut at specific recognition sites using restriction endonucleases. Third, the resulting fragments are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, and the desired DNA fragment is isolated (eluted) from the gel. Fourth, this purified target fragment is joined with a cut cloning vector using DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA. Finally, the recombinant DNA molecule is introduced into a competent host cell for replication and expression.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: isolation of pure DNA, fragmentation by restriction endonucleases, isolation of the desired fragment via electrophoresis, ligation into a vector, and transfer into the host organism.

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Sacred groves as in-situ biodiversity conservation

questiontext.text: Which of the following regions in India is a well-known example of sacred groves, where tracts of forest are set aside and all the trees and wildlife within are venerated and given total protection?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity conservation can be achieved through in-situ (on-site) or ex-situ (off-site) approaches. Sacred groves represent a traditional form of in-situ conservation in India, in which patches of forest are protected by local communities due to cultural and religious beliefs.

Step 2: Evaluation
In India, sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda, and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh. By contrast, Kaziranga and Manas in Assam, the Sundarbans in West Bengal, and Silent Valley in Kerala are designated national parks or biosphere reserves rather than community-venerated sacred groves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The region that exemplifies sacred groves in India is the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya.

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Intrinsic rate of natural increase calculation

questiontext.text: In a freshwater pond, a population of \(800\) Hydrilla individuals experiences \(120\) new individuals added through natality and \(40\) individuals lost through mortality over a period of one year, while immigration equals emigration. Assuming unlimited resources and constant per capita birth and death rates, what are the intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) and the net population size (\(N\)) at the end of that year?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial population size, \(N_0 = 800\).
Number of births in one year, \(B = 120\).
Number of deaths in one year, \(D = 40\).
Time interval, \(\Delta t = 1\text{ year}\).
Immigration equals emigration (\(I = E\)), so net migration is zero.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Natality contributes positively to population growth, whereas mortality contributes negatively. Under unlimited resources, growth follows the exponential model with constant per capita birth rate \(b\) and per capita death rate \(d\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Per capita birth rate: \(b = \frac{B}{N_0}\)
Per capita death rate: \(d = \frac{D}{N_0}\)
Intrinsic rate of natural increase: \(r = b - d\)
Net change in population over one year: \(\Delta N = r N_0 = B - D\)
Final population size: \(N = N_0 + \Delta N\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the per capita birth rate:
\[b = \frac{120}{800} = 0.15\text{ year}^{-1}\]
Calculate the per capita death rate:
\[d = \frac{40}{800} = 0.05\text{ year}^{-1}\]
Calculate the intrinsic rate of natural increase:
\[r = b - d = 0.15 - 0.05 = 0.10\text{ year}^{-1}\]
Calculate the net increase in population size:
\[\Delta N = r N_0 = 0.10 \times 800 = 80\]
Calculate the population size at the end of one year:
\[N = 800 + 80 = 880\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking via direct count balance: \(N = 800 + 120 - 40 = 880\), which matches the rate-based calculation, and \(r = 0.10\text{ year}^{-1}\) is positive as births exceed deaths. Therefore, \(r = 0.10\text{ year}^{-1}\) and \(N = 880\).

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q03 - Ecological pyramids of energy and biomass

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, the pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted.

Statement II: In a deep ocean ecosystem, the pyramid of biomass is typically upright because the standing crop of phytoplankton exceeds that of zooplankton and fishes at any given instant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ecological pyramids represent trophic structure in terms of number, biomass, or energy. According to the second law of thermodynamics and the \(10\%\) energy transfer law, energy flows unidirectionally from lower to higher trophic levels, with substantial energy lost as heat at every transfer.

Step 2: Evaluation of Energy Pyramid
Because energy is progressively lost as heat during respiration and metabolic activities at each successive trophic level, the total energy available at a lower trophic level is always greater than that at the next higher trophic level. Hence, the pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted.

Step 3: Evaluation of Marine Biomass Pyramid
In a deep ocean or sea ecosystem, the pyramid of biomass is generally inverted rather than upright. At any given instant, the standing crop (biomass) of fishes and zooplankton far exceeds the standing crop of phytoplankton, because phytoplankton have a very short lifespan and a rapid turnover rate that supports a larger consumer biomass over time.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The principle describing the pyramid of energy as always upright is correct, whereas the claim describing the deep ocean pyramid of biomass as upright is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MULTISTATEMENT_Q04 - Population interactions and ecological principles

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements regarding population interactions and choose the option that identifies all the correct statements:

A. In brood parasitism, the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host, and during evolution the eggs of the parasitic bird have evolved to resemble the host's eggs in size and colour.

B. According to Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle, two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources can coexist indefinitely if resources are abundant.

C. In mutualism between fig trees and pollinator wasps, the wasp uses the fruit not only as an oviposition site but also uses the developing seeds within the fruit for nourishing its larvae.

D. Predators help in maintaining species diversity in a community by increasing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.

E. MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and coexist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Species in a community interact through parasitism, competition, mutualism, and predation, shaping population dynamics, co-evolution, and species coexistence.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Ecological Claim
In brood parasitism (such as the cuckoo and the crow), the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the host's nest, and evolutionary selection favours parasitic eggs that closely mimic the host's eggs in size and colour to reduce detection; this claim is correct.
Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will eventually be eliminated if resources are limiting; claiming they can coexist indefinitely under limiting resources contradicts the principle, making this claim incorrect.
In the obligate mutualism between fig trees and pollinator wasps, the female wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites, and the developing seeds nourish the wasp larvae; this claim is correct.
Predators maintain species diversity in a community by reducing (not increasing) the intensity of competition among competing prey species, preventing any single prey species from dominating; therefore, claiming they increase competition is incorrect.
MacArthur's classic study on five closely related warbler species on the same tree demonstrated resource partitioning through behavioural differences in foraging activities, enabling coexistence; this claim is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding brood parasitism egg mimicry, fig-wasp mutualism, and MacArthur's warbler resource partitioning are correct.

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Logistic population growth rate and carrying capacity

questiontext.text:
Observe the population growth curves shown below, where Curve \(P\) represents exponential growth and Curve \(Q\) represents Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth with carrying capacity \(K = 1200\).

If the intrinsic rate of natural increase is \(r = 0.4\text{ year}^{-1}\), at what population density \(N\) on Curve \(Q\) is the population growth rate \(\frac{dN}{dt}\) maximum, and what is that maximum growth rate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the growth-curve diagram, the horizontal asymptote representing the carrying capacity of the habitat is \(K = 1200\).
The intrinsic rate of natural increase is \(r = 0.4\text{ year}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The sigmoid curve follows the Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth model, where environmental resistance increases as population density \(N\) approaches carrying capacity \(K\), and \(N\) is constrained within \(0 < N \le K\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth equation is:
\[\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K - N}{K}\right)\]
Since \(\frac{dN}{dt}\) is a downward-opening quadratic function of \(N\) with roots at \(N = 0\) and \(N = K\), its maximum occurs at the inflection point of the sigmoid curve, where:
\[N = \frac{K}{2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Find the population density at maximum growth rate:
\[N = \frac{1200}{2} = 600\]
Substitute \(r = 0.4\text{ year}^{-1}\), \(N = 600\), and \(K = 1200\) into the logistic growth rate equation:
\[\left(\frac{dN}{dt}\right)_{\max} = 0.4 \times 600 \times \left(\frac{1200 - 600}{1200}\right)\]
\[\left(\frac{dN}{dt}\right)_{\max} = 240 \times \frac{600}{1200} = 240 \times 0.5 = 120\text{ individuals year}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with the shortcut \(\left(\frac{dN}{dt}\right)_{\max} = \frac{rK}{4} = \frac{0.4 \times 1200}{4} = 120\text{ individuals year}^{-1}\) confirms the result, and \(N = 600\) lies strictly at half the carrying capacity. Thus, the maximum growth rate occurs at \(N = 600\) and equals \(120\text{ individuals year}^{-1}\).

name.text: [ch010-unit-10-ecology-and-environment] NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Sequential steps of detritus decomposition

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of the five key steps involved in the decomposition of detritus in a terrestrial ecosystem, from the initial breakdown of detritus to the release of inorganic nutrients?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Decomposition is the biological and physical process by which complex organic matter (detritus) is broken down into simpler inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water, and mineral nutrients.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Sequential Stages
First, fragmentation occurs when detritivores (such as earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles, increasing the surface area for microbial action.
Next, leaching takes place as water-soluble inorganic nutrients percolate down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
Then, catabolism is carried out by bacterial and fungal enzymes that degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.
Subsequently, humification leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes at an extremely slow rate.
Finally, mineralisation occurs when humus is further degraded by certain microbes, resulting in the release of inorganic nutrients back into the soil.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of decomposition steps is Fragmentation \(\rightarrow\) Leaching \(\rightarrow\) Catabolism \(\rightarrow\) Humification \(\rightarrow\) Mineralisation.
